# 06. Agents, skills and tools

## What it is

In complex mode Hive runs opencode with oh-my-openagent, which adds named agents and task categories. Hive also installs two skills and three tools (graphify, Playwright MCP, OpenSpec). All of this is installed by `habithive setup`. Hive does not bundle opencode or oh-my-openagent; it installs them from their official sources.

## Agents

oh-my-openagent has four main agents and seven subagents. Hive's model tree (`/hive-models`) lists exactly these.

Main agents are primary modes. You switch between them in the TUI and they use the model selected on screen.

| Agent | Role |
|-------|------|
| `sisyphus` | Ultraworker, the default orchestrating agent |
| `prometheus` | Plan builder |
| `atlas` | Plan executor |
| `hephaestus` | Deep worker, GPT models only |

Subagents are started by other agents through tasks. Each has its own model in `~/.config/opencode/oh-my-openagent.json`.

| Agent | Role |
|-------|------|
| `oracle` | Deep reasoning and debugging |
| `explore` | Codebase search |
| `librarian` | External documentation |
| `multimodal-looker` | Images and visual input |
| `metis` | Plan consultant |
| `momus` | Plan critic |
| `sisyphus-junior` | Worker |

## Categories

Categories are task tiers. An agent delegating work picks a category, and the category decides the model. oh-my-openagent defines eight:

`ultrabrain`, `deep`, `quick`, `visual-engineering`, `artistry`, `writing`, `unspecified-low`, `unspecified-high`.

Model precedence in the tree: agent override, then category override, then the "everything" override, then your baseline. See [03-model-tree.md](03-model-tree.md).

## GPT rules

oh-my-openagent enforces two rules through its own hooks. Hive does not change them. It warns you before a relaunch if your chosen model will be rerouted.

| Agent | Rule |
|-------|------|
| Sisyphus | Cannot use older GPT models. Models from `gpt-5.4` upward and the `gpt-5.x-codex` models are accepted. Otherwise the session is switched to Hephaestus. |
| Hephaestus | Requires a GPT model. With a non-GPT model it shows an error and the session returns to Sisyphus (oh-my-openagent 4.19.1). It is also absent from the agent list. |

To allow a non-GPT model on Hephaestus, set `agents.hephaestus.allow_non_gpt_model: true` in `oh-my-openagent.json`. Hive reads this setting and then does not warn. See [../COMPATIBILITY.md](../COMPATIBILITY.md) (finding 12).

## Bundled skills

Setup copies the skills in the package's `skills/` folder to `~/.config/opencode/skills/`, replacing earlier copies. oh-my-openagent loads them in complex mode.

| Skill | For | Triggers |
|-------|-----|----------|
| `karpathy-guidelines` | Reducing common LLM coding mistakes: avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, state assumptions, define verifiable success criteria | When the agent writes, reviews or refactors code (matched by its description) |
| `graphify` | Turning code, docs, papers, images or video into a knowledge graph, and answering codebase questions from it | `/graphify`, or any codebase question, especially when `graphify-out/` exists |

`karpathy-guidelines` is bundled unmodified under the MIT licence from the andrej-karpathy-skills project.

## graphify CLI

The `graphify` skill drives the `graphify` command-line tool, published on PyPI as `graphifyy`. graphify needs Python 3.10 or newer. Setup installs it with `uv tool install --upgrade graphifyy`, or with `pip install -U graphifyy` when `uv` is missing and Python is 3.10+. On an older Python, such as macOS's built-in 3.9, setup installs `uv` with Homebrew: uv brings its own Python for graphify and leaves the system Python alone. Without Homebrew, setup skips graphify and says so. If `uv` already manages it, setup runs `uv tool upgrade graphifyy`. If the `graphify` command is not on your PATH afterwards, run `uv tool update-shell` and open a new terminal. It builds an interactive HTML graph, a JSON graph and a `GRAPH_REPORT.md`.

```text
/graphify                 # graph of the current folder
/graphify <path> --update # re-extract only changed files
```

The skill was written for Claude Code's subagent runtime and may need tuning under opencode.

## Playwright MCP

Gives agents a real browser to open pages, click, fill forms and take screenshots. Setup adds this entry to `mcp` in `opencode.jsonc` (in each mode's config) if it is not there:

```json
"playwright": { "type": "local", "enabled": true, "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest"] }
```

An existing entry is kept as you wrote it. The package is fetched by `npx` on first use.

## OpenSpec CLI

Installed at the pinned version 1.5.0, with the `intent-driven` schema. See [05-spec-workflow.md](05-spec-workflow.md).

## Licences and credits

Hive installs opencode, oh-my-openagent, OpenSpec, graphify and Playwright MCP from their official sources under their own licences. Bundled skills and their licence texts are listed in [../../THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md](../../THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). Project overview: [../../README.md](../../README.md).

# /graphify

Turn any folder of files into a navigable knowledge graph with community detection, an honest audit trail, and three outputs: interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, and a plain-language GRAPH_REPORT.md.

## Usage

```
/graphify                                             # full pipeline on current directory → Obsidian vault
/graphify <path>                                      # full pipeline on specific path
/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>           # clone repo then run full pipeline on it
/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> --branch <branch>  # clone a specific branch
/graphify <url1> <url2> ...                           # clone multiple repos, build each, merge into one cross-repo graph
/graphify <path> --mode deep                          # thorough extraction, richer INFERRED edges
/graphify <path> --update                             # incremental - re-extract only new/changed files
/graphify <path> --directed                            # build directed graph (preserves edge direction: source→target)
/graphify <path> --whisper-model medium                # use a larger Whisper model for better transcription accuracy
/graphify <path> --cluster-only                       # rerun clustering on existing graph
/graphify <path> --no-viz                             # skip visualization, just report + JSON
/graphify <path> --html                               # (HTML is generated by default - this flag is a no-op)
/graphify <path> --svg                                # also export graph.svg (embeds in Notion, GitHub)
/graphify <path> --graphml                            # export graph.graphml (Gephi, yEd)
/graphify <path> --neo4j                              # generate graphify-out/cypher.txt for Neo4j
/graphify <path> --neo4j-push bolt://localhost:7687   # push directly to Neo4j
/graphify <path> --mcp                                # start MCP stdio server for agent access
/graphify <path> --watch                              # watch folder, auto-rebuild on code changes (no LLM needed)
/graphify <path> --wiki                               # build agent-crawlable wiki (index.md + one article per community)
/graphify <path> --obsidian --obsidian-dir ~/vaults/my-project  # write vault to custom path (e.g. existing vault)
/graphify add <url>                                   # fetch URL, save to ./raw, update graph
/graphify add <url> --author "Name"                   # tag who wrote it
/graphify add <url> --contributor "Name"              # tag who added it to the corpus
/graphify query "<question>"                          # BFS traversal - broad context
/graphify query "<question>" --dfs                    # DFS - trace a specific path
/graphify query "<question>" --budget 1500            # cap answer at N tokens
/graphify path "AuthModule" "Database"                # shortest path between two concepts
/graphify explain "SwinTransformer"                   # plain-language explanation of a node
```

## What graphify is for

Drop any folder of code, docs, papers, images, or video into graphify and get a queryable knowledge graph. Persistent across sessions, honest audit trail (EXTRACTED/INFERRED/AMBIGUOUS), community detection surfaces cross-document connections you wouldn't think to ask about.

## What You Must Do When Invoked

If the user invoked `/graphify --help` or `/graphify -h` (with no other arguments), print the contents of the `## Usage` section above verbatim and stop. Do not run any commands, do not detect files, do not default the path to `.`. Just print the Usage block and return.

**Fast path — existing graph:** Before doing anything else, check whether `graphify-out/graph.json` exists. The expected location is `graphify-out/graph.json` relative to the **current working directory** (i.e. the project root where you are running commands). If it exists AND the user's request is a natural-language question about the codebase (e.g. "How does X work?", "What calls Y?", "Trace the data flow through Z") and NOT an explicit rebuild command (`--update`, `--cluster-only`, or a bare path/URL that implies fresh extraction): **skip Steps 1–5 entirely and jump straight to `## For /graphify query`.** Run `graphify query "<question>"` immediately. Do not run detect. Do not check corpus size. Do not ask the user to narrow. The graph is already built — use it.

If no path was given, use `.` (current directory). Do not ask the user for a path.

If the path argument starts with `https://github.com/` or `http://github.com/`, treat it as a GitHub URL - run Step 0 before anything else, then continue with the resolved local path.

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.

### Step 0 - Clone GitHub repo(s) (only if a GitHub URL was given)

**Single repo:**
```bash
LOCAL_PATH=$(graphify clone <github-url> [--branch <branch>])
# Use LOCAL_PATH as the target for all subsequent steps
```

**Multiple repos (cross-repo graph):**
```bash
# Clone each repo, run the full pipeline on each, then merge
graphify clone <url1>   # → ~/.graphify/repos/<owner1>/<repo1>
graphify clone <url2>   # → ~/.graphify/repos/<owner2>/<repo2>
# Run /graphify on each local path to produce their graph.json files
# Then merge:
graphify merge-graphs \
  ~/.graphify/repos/<owner1>/<repo1>/graphify-out/graph.json \
  ~/.graphify/repos/<owner2>/<repo2>/graphify-out/graph.json \
  --out graphify-out/cross-repo-graph.json
```

Graphify clones into `~/.graphify/repos/<owner>/<repo>` and reuses existing clones on repeat runs. Each node in the merged graph carries a `repo` attribute so you can filter by origin.

**Multiple local subfolders (monorepo or multi-service layout):**

The skill pipeline writes all intermediate and final outputs to `graphify-out/` in the current working directory. Running the skill on each subfolder separately will clobber the same output dir. Instead, use the CLI directly for each subfolder — it places `graphify-out/` *inside* the scanned path:

```bash
graphify extract ./core/     # → ./core/graphify-out/graph.json
graphify extract ./service/  # → ./service/graphify-out/graph.json
graphify extract ./platform/ # → ./platform/graphify-out/graph.json
# Add --backend gemini|kimi|openai|deepseek|claude-cli depending on which API key you have set

# Then merge at the project root:
graphify merge-graphs \
  ./core/graphify-out/graph.json \
  ./service/graphify-out/graph.json \
  ./platform/graphify-out/graph.json \
  --out graphify-out/graph.json
```

Once `graphify-out/graph.json` exists, the fast path above takes over: any codebase question runs `graphify query` directly on the merged graph — no re-extraction, no size gate.

### Step 1 - Ensure graphify is installed

```bash
# Detect the correct Python interpreter (handles uv tool, pipx, venv, system installs)
PYTHON=""
GRAPHIFY_BIN=$(which graphify 2>/dev/null)
# 1. uv tool installs — most reliable on modern Mac/Linux
if [ -z "$PYTHON" ] && command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    _UV_PY=$(uv tool run graphifyy python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" 2>/dev/null)
    if [ -n "$_UV_PY" ]; then PYTHON="$_UV_PY"; fi
fi
# 2. Read shebang from graphify binary (pipx and direct pip installs)
if [ -z "$PYTHON" ] && [ -n "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" ]; then
    _SHEBANG=$(head -1 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" | tr -d '#!')
    case "$_SHEBANG" in
        *[!a-zA-Z0-9/_.-]*) ;;
        *) "$_SHEBANG" -c "import graphify" 2>/dev/null && PYTHON="$_SHEBANG" ;;
    esac
fi
# 3. Fall back to python3
if [ -z "$PYTHON" ]; then PYTHON="python3"; fi
if ! "$PYTHON" -c "import graphify" 2>/dev/null; then
    if command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        uv tool install --upgrade graphifyy -q 2>&1 | tail -3
        _UV_PY=$(uv tool run graphifyy python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" 2>/dev/null)
        if [ -n "$_UV_PY" ]; then PYTHON="$_UV_PY"; fi
    else
        "$PYTHON" -m pip install graphifyy -q 2>/dev/null \
          || "$PYTHON" -m pip install graphifyy -q --break-system-packages 2>&1 | tail -3
    fi
fi
# Write interpreter path for all subsequent steps (persists across invocations)
mkdir -p graphify-out
"$PYTHON" -c "import sys; open('graphify-out/.graphify_python', 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(sys.executable)"
# Save scan root so `graphify update` (no args) knows where to look next time
echo "$(cd INPUT_PATH && pwd)" > graphify-out/.graphify_root
```

If the import succeeds, print nothing and move straight to Step 2.

**In every subsequent bash block, replace `python3` with `$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python)` to use the correct interpreter.**

### Step 2 - Detect files

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json
from graphify.detect import detect
from pathlib import Path
result = detect(Path('INPUT_PATH'))
print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False))
" > graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json
```

Replace INPUT_PATH with the actual path the user provided. Do NOT cat or print the JSON - read it silently and present a clean summary instead:

```
Corpus: X files · ~Y words
  code:     N files (.py .ts .go ...)
  docs:     N files (.md .txt ...)
  papers:   N files (.pdf ...)
  images:   N files
  video:    N files (.mp4 .mp3 ...)
```

Omit any category with 0 files from the summary.

Then act on it:
- If `total_files` is 0: stop with "No supported files found in [path]."
- If `skipped_sensitive` is non-empty: mention file count skipped, not the file names.
- If `total_words` > 2,000,000 OR `total_files` > 500: show the warning. Then compute the top 5 first-level subdirectories by file count:
  - Read `scan_root` from the detect JSON (always an absolute path to the resolved INPUT_PATH).
  - Concatenate all file lists across all types (`code`, `document`, `paper`, `image`, `video`).
  - Filter out any path that starts with `scan_root + "/graphify-out/"` to exclude converted sidecars.
  - For each file, strip the `scan_root` prefix and take the first path component. Files directly in `scan_root` with no subdirectory count as `(root)`.
  - If all files are in `(root)` with no subdirectories, do not ask to narrow — no subfolders exist. Instead suggest `--no-cluster` to skip the expensive clustering step and proceed.
  - Otherwise rank by count, show the top 5 with file counts, then ask which subfolder to run on. Wait for the user's answer before proceeding.
- Otherwise: proceed directly to Step 2.5 if video files were detected, or Step 3 if not.

### Step 2.5 - Transcribe video / audio files (only if video files detected)

Skip this step entirely if `detect` returned zero `video` files.

Video and audio files cannot be read directly. Transcribe them to text first, then treat the transcripts as doc files in Step 3.

**Strategy:** Read the god nodes from `graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json` (or the analysis file if it exists from a previous run). You are already a language model — write a one-sentence domain hint yourself from those labels. Then pass it to Whisper as the initial prompt. No separate API call needed.

**However**, if the corpus has *only* video files and no other docs/code, use the generic fallback prompt: `"Use proper punctuation and paragraph breaks."`

**Step 1 - Write the Whisper prompt yourself.**

Read the top god node labels from detect output or analysis, then compose a short domain hint sentence, for example:

- Labels: `transformer, attention, encoder, decoder` → `"Machine learning research on transformer architectures and attention mechanisms. Use proper punctuation and paragraph breaks."`
- Labels: `kubernetes, deployment, pod, helm` → `"DevOps discussion about Kubernetes deployments and Helm charts. Use proper punctuation and paragraph breaks."`

Set it as `WHISPER_PROMPT` to use in the next command.

**Step 2 - Transcribe:**

```bash
GRAPHIFY_WHISPER_MODEL=base  # or whatever --whisper-model the user passed
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json, os
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.transcribe import transcribe_all

detect = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
video_files = detect.get('files', {}).get('video', [])
prompt = os.environ.get('GRAPHIFY_WHISPER_PROMPT', 'Use proper punctuation and paragraph breaks.')

transcript_paths = transcribe_all(video_files, initial_prompt=prompt)
print(json.dumps(transcript_paths, ensure_ascii=False))
" > graphify-out/.graphify_transcripts.json
```

After transcription:
- Read the transcript paths from `graphify-out/.graphify_transcripts.json`
- Add them to the docs list before dispatching semantic subagents in Step 3B
- Print how many transcripts were created: `Transcribed N video file(s) -> treating as docs`
- If transcription fails for a file, print a warning and continue with the rest

**Whisper model:** Default is `base`. If the user passed `--whisper-model <name>`, set `GRAPHIFY_WHISPER_MODEL=<name>` in the environment before running the command above.

### Step 3 - Extract entities and relationships

**Before starting:** note whether `--mode deep` was given. You must pass `DEEP_MODE=true` to every subagent in Step B2 if it was. Track this from the original invocation - do not lose it.

This step has two parts: **structural extraction** (deterministic, free) and **semantic extraction** (LLM, costs tokens).

> **Model:** All semantic extraction uses Claude (claude-sonnet-4-6) subagents exclusively. Gemini and all other third-party backends are disabled. Do not check for `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, or any other provider key — always dispatch Claude subagents as described in Part B below.

**Run Part A (AST) and Part B (semantic) in parallel. Dispatch all semantic subagents AND start AST extraction in the same message. Both can run simultaneously since they operate on different file types. Merge results in Part C as before.**

Note: Parallelizing AST + semantic saves 5-15s on large corpora. AST is deterministic and fast; start it while subagents are processing docs/papers.

#### Part A - Structural extraction for code files

For any code files detected, run AST extraction in parallel with Part B subagents:

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import sys, json
from graphify.extract import collect_files, extract
from pathlib import Path
import json

code_files = []
detect = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
for f in detect.get('files', {}).get('code', []):
    code_files.extend(collect_files(Path(f)) if Path(f).is_dir() else [Path(f)])

if code_files:
    result = extract(code_files, cache_root=Path('.'))
    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json').write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
    print(f'AST: {len(result[\"nodes\"])} nodes, {len(result[\"edges\"])} edges')
else:
    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json').write_text(json.dumps({'nodes':[],'edges':[],'input_tokens':0,'output_tokens':0}, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
    print('No code files - skipping AST extraction')
"
```

#### Part B - Semantic extraction (parallel subagents)

**Fast path:** If detection found zero docs, papers, and images (code-only corpus), skip Part B entirely and go straight to Part C. AST handles code - there is nothing for semantic subagents to do.

**MANDATORY: You MUST use the Agent tool here. Reading files yourself one-by-one is forbidden - it is 5-10x slower. If you do not use the Agent tool you are doing this wrong.**

Before dispatching subagents, print a timing estimate:
- Load `total_words` and file counts from `graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json`
- Estimate agents needed: `ceil(uncached_non_code_files / 22)` (chunk size is 20-25)
- Estimate time: ~45s per agent batch (they run in parallel, so total ≈ 45s × ceil(agents/parallel_limit))
- Print: "Semantic extraction: ~N files → X agents, estimated ~Ys"

**Step B0 - Check extraction cache first**

Before dispatching any subagents, check which files already have cached extraction results:

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json
from graphify.cache import check_semantic_cache
from path
…[文件过长——中段 8KB 抽样]…
 regardless of which chunk processes it.

Generate the extraction JSON matching this schema exactly:
{"nodes":[{"id":"session_validatetoken","label":"Human Readable Name","file_type":"code|document|paper|image|rationale|concept","source_file":"relative/path","source_location":null,"source_url":null,"captured_at":null,"author":null,"contributor":null}],"edges":[{"source":"node_id","target":"node_id","relation":"calls|implements|references|cites|conceptually_related_to|shares_data_with|semantically_similar_to|rationale_for","confidence":"EXTRACTED|INFERRED|AMBIGUOUS","confidence_score":1.0,"source_file":"relative/path","source_location":null,"weight":1.0}],"hyperedges":[{"id":"snake_case_id","label":"Human Readable Label","nodes":["node_id1","node_id2","node_id3"],"relation":"participate_in|implement|form","confidence":"EXTRACTED|INFERRED","confidence_score":0.75,"source_file":"relative/path"}],"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0}

Then write the JSON to disk using the Write tool at this exact absolute path (no relative paths — Write resolves relative paths against an undefined cwd and the file will be silently lost):
CHUNK_PATH
```

**Step B3 - Collect, cache, and merge**

Wait for all subagents. For each result:
- Check that `graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_NN.json` exists on disk — this is the success signal
- If the file exists and contains valid JSON with `nodes` and `edges`, include it and save to cache
- If the file is missing, the subagent was likely dispatched as read-only (Explore type) — print a warning: "chunk N missing from disk — subagent may have been read-only. Re-run with general-purpose agent." Do not silently skip.
- If a subagent failed or returned invalid JSON, print a warning and skip that chunk - do not abort

If more than half the chunks failed or are missing, stop and tell the user to re-run and ensure `subagent_type="general-purpose"` is used.

Merge all chunk files into `.graphify_semantic_new.json`. **After each Agent call completes, read the real token counts from the Agent tool result's `usage` field and write them back into the chunk JSON before merging** — the chunk JSON itself always has placeholder zeros. Then run:
```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json, glob
from pathlib import Path

chunks = sorted(glob.glob('graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_*.json'))
all_nodes, all_edges, all_hyperedges = [], [], []
total_in, total_out = 0, 0
for c in chunks:
    d = json.loads(Path(c).read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
    all_nodes += d.get('nodes', [])
    all_edges += d.get('edges', [])
    all_hyperedges += d.get('hyperedges', [])
    total_in += d.get('input_tokens', 0)
    total_out += d.get('output_tokens', 0)
Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').write_text(json.dumps({
    'nodes': all_nodes, 'edges': all_edges, 'hyperedges': all_hyperedges,
    'input_tokens': total_in, 'output_tokens': total_out,
}, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
print(f'Merged {len(chunks)} chunks: {total_in:,} in / {total_out:,} out tokens')
"
```

Save new results to cache:
```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json
from graphify.cache import save_semantic_cache
from pathlib import Path

new = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")) if Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').exists() else {'nodes':[],'edges':[],'hyperedges':[]}
saved = save_semantic_cache(new.get('nodes', []), new.get('edges', []), new.get('hyperedges', []))
print(f'Cached {saved} files')
"
```

Merge cached + new results into `graphify-out/.graphify_semantic.json`:
```bash

If the user's question uses different language or different domain vocabulary than the graph's labels (user says "обработчик" / graph says "handler"; user says "authentication" / graph says "Guardian"), the literal matcher returns 0 hits and the answer collapses to noise.

Fix this **without inventing tokens** by expanding the query against the actual graph vocabulary first:

1. Extract the token vocabulary from node labels:
```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import json, re
from pathlib import Path
data = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/graph.json').read_text())
vocab = set()
for n in data['nodes']:
    for c in re.findall(r'[^\W\d_]+', n.get('label','') or '', re.UNICODE):
        parts = re.findall(r'[A-Z]+(?=[A-Z][a-z])|[A-Z]?[a-z]+|[A-Z]+', c) or [c]
        for p in parts:
            t = p.lower()
            if 3 <= len(t) <= 30:
                vocab.add(t)
Path('graphify-out/.vocab.txt').write_text('\n'.join(sorted(vocab)))
print(f'vocab: {len(vocab)} tokens')
"
```

2. Read `graphify-out/.vocab.txt`. Then for the user's question, select **up to 12 tokens from this exact list** that semantically match the query intent. Hard constraints:
   - You MUST pick only tokens present in the vocabulary file. Do NOT invent tokens.
   - If a query concept has no plausible token in the vocab, skip it — do not substitute a near-synonym from training memory.
   - If **no** vocab tokens match the query at all, output an empty list and tell the user the corpus has no relevant vocabulary for this question. Do not fabricate a search.
   - Translate cross-language: Russian "аутентификация" → look for `auth`, `credential`, `token`, `security` IFF present in vocab.
   - Morphology: "handlers" maps to `handler` IFF present; "todos" maps to `todo` IFF present.

3. Print the selection explicitly to the user before running the query, so the expansion is auditable:
```
Query expanded to (from graph vocab, N tokens): [token1, token2, ...]
```
If the list is empty, say so plainly and stop — do not proceed to traversal.

### Step 1 — Traversal

Build the **expanded query string** by joining the selected tokens with spaces. Use this string as `QUESTION` below — NOT the original user question. (The original question is preserved only for `save-result` at the end.)

```bash
graphify query "QUESTION"
# or: graphify query "QUESTION" --dfs --budget 3000
```

Answer using **only** what the graph output contains. Quote `source_location` when citing a specific fact. If the graph lacks enough information, say so - do not hallucinate edges.

After writing the answer, save it back into the graph so it improves future queries. Include the expanded tokens inside the `--answer` text (e.g. `"Expanded from original query via vocab: [tokens]. Then traversed..."`) so the next `--update` extracts the expansion history as a graph node:

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -m graphify save-result --question "ORIGINAL_QUESTION" --answer "ANSWER" --type query --nodes NODE1 NODE2
```

Replace `ORIGINAL_QUESTION` with the user's verbatim question, `ANSWER` with your full answer text (containing the expanded-token trace), `NODE1 NODE2` with the list of node labels you cited. This closes the feedback loop: the next `--update` will extract this Q&A as a node in the graph.

Find the shortest path between two named concepts in the graph.

Replace `NODE_A` and `NODE_B` with the actual concept names. Then explain the path in plain language - what each hop means, why it's significant.

After writing the explanation, save it back:

```bash

## For /graphify explain

Give a plain-language explanation of a single node - everything connected to it.

```bash
graphify explain "NODE_NAME"
```

Replace `NODE_NAME` with the concept the user asked about. Then write a 3-5 sentence explanation of what this node is, what it connects to, and why those connections are significant. Use the source locations as citations.

After writing the explanation, save it back:

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -m graphify save-result --question "Explain NODE_NAME" --answer "ANSWER" --type explain --nodes NODE_NAME
```

## For /graphify add

Fetch a URL and add it to the corpus, then update the graph.

```bash
$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
import sys
from graphify.ingest import ingest
from pathlib import Path

try:
    out = ingest('URL', Path('./raw'), author='AUTHOR', contributor='CONTRIBUTOR')
    print(f'Saved to {out}')
except ValueError as e:
    print(f'error: {e}', file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f'error: {e}', file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
"
```

Replace `URL` with the actual URL, `AUTHOR` with the user's name if provided, `CONTRIBUTOR` likewise. If the command exits with an error, tell the user what went wrong - do not silently continue. After a successful save, automatically run the `--update` pipeline on `./raw` to merge the new file into the existing graph.

Supported URL types (auto-detected):
- YouTube / any video URL → audio downloaded via yt-dlp, transcribed to `.txt` on next run (requires `pip install 'graphifyy[video]'`)
- Twitter/X → fetched via oEmbed, saved as `.md` with tweet text and author
- arXiv → abstract + metadata saved as `.md`
- PDF → downloaded as `.pdf`
- Images (.png/.jpg/.webp) → downloaded, Claude vision extracts on next run
- Any webpage → converted to markdown via html2text

## For --watch

Start a background watcher that monitors a folder and auto-updates the graph when files change.

```bash
python3 -m graphify.watch INPUT_PATH --debounce 3
```

Replace INPUT_PATH with the folder to watch. Behavior depends on what changed:

- **Code files only (.py, .ts, .go, etc.):** re-runs AST extraction + rebuild + cluster immediately, no LLM needed. `graph.json` and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` are updated automatically.
- **Docs, papers, or images:** writes a `graphify-out/needs_update` flag and prints a notification to run `/graphify --update` (LLM semantic re-extraction required).

Debounce (default 3s): waits until file activity stops before triggering, so a wave of parallel agent writes doesn't trigger a rebuild per file.

Press Ctrl+C to stop.

For agentic workflows: run `--watch` in a background terminal. Code changes from agent waves are picked up automatically between waves. If agents are also writing docs or notes, you'll need a manual `/graphify --update` after those waves.

---

## For git commit hook

Install a post-commit hook that auto-rebuilds the graph after every commit. No background process needed - triggers once per commit, works with any editor.

```bash
graphify hook install    # install
graphify hook uninstall  # remove
graphify hook status     # check
```

After every `git commit`, the hook detects which code files changed (via `git diff HEAD~1`), re-runs AST extraction on those files, and rebuilds `graph.json` and `GRAPH_REPORT.md`. Doc/image changes are ignored by the hook - run `/graphify --update` manually for those.

If a post-commit hook already exists, graphify appends to it rather than replacing it.

---

## For native CLAUDE.md integration

Run once per project to make graphify always-on in Claude Code sessions:

```bash
graphify claude install
```

This writes a `## graphify` section to the local `CLAUDE.md` that instructs Claude to check the graph before answering codebase questions and rebuild it after code changes. No manual `/graphify` needed in future sessions.

```bash
graphify claude uninstall  # remove the section
```

## Honesty Rules

- Never invent an edge. If unsure, use AMBIGUOUS.
- Never skip the corpus check warning.
- Always show token cost in the report.
- Never hide cohesion scores behind symbols - show the raw number.
- Never run HTML viz on a graph with more than 5,000 nodes without warning the user.

# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

# habithive-code (Hive)

Hive is a control layer for [opencode](https://github.com/sst/opencode). It gives you a one-command install, live switching between simple and complex mode, a model tree for the [oh-my-openagent](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent) agents, an OmniRoute provider, a spec workflow (OpenSpec with the `intent-driven` schema), and a few bundled skills and tools.

Hive does not bundle opencode or oh-my-openagent. It installs them from their official sources under their own licenses. The command is `habithive`; `hive` is the same command.

## Quick start

Prerequisites: Node.js 20.19 or newer (for example `nvm install 22`) and internet access for the first setup.

```sh
npm i -g habithive-code
habithive setup          # installs and wires everything
habithive                # complex mode, new session
```

To use OmniRoute, enable it once with the gateway address your team gives you, then add your key inside opencode:

```sh
habithive --gateway <ip>      # Hive adds http:// and port 20128
# in opencode: /connect -> OmniRoute -> paste your key
```

Full walk-through: [Getting started](docs/guide/01-getting-started.md).

## What you get

| Component | What it is | Where it comes from |
|-----------|------------|---------------------|
| opencode | The coding agent, pinned to the tested version | npm `opencode-ai` |
| oh-my-openagent | Agent harness that complex mode enables, pinned | npm `oh-my-openagent@4.19.1` |
| Hive TUI plugin | Wordmark, `/habithive` menu, model tree, mode switch | this package |
| Playwright MCP | Browser tools for agents (`@playwright/mcp`) | added to the opencode `mcp` config |
| OpenSpec + intent-driven schema | Spec CLI pinned at **1.5.0**, plus the team schema | npm `@fission-ai/openspec`; schema shipped here |
| graphify | Knowledge-graph CLI (`graphifyy`, needs Python 3.10+) | PyPI, via `uv` (installed with Homebrew if needed) or `pip` |
| Bundled skills | `karpathy-guidelines` and `graphify` | `skills/` in this package |
| OmniRoute | Provider with 38 `auto/*` models | written into both modes' config |

OpenSpec is pinned at **1.5.0** because newer releases reject the `intent-driven` schema. The Node 20.19 minimum comes from OpenSpec. There is no minimal install: setup always installs everything.

## Compatibility

Each release is tested against exactly one opencode and one oh-my-openagent version (defined in `src/versions.js`).

| Component | Tested version |
|-----------|----------------|
| opencode (`OPENCODE_PIN`) | **1.19.4** |
| oh-my-openagent (`OMO_SPEC`) | **4.19.1** (5.x is not supported yet) |

`habithive setup` installs opencode 1.19.4, or moves an existing install to it: `npm i -g opencode-ai@1.19.4` for an npm install, `opencode upgrade 1.19.4` for Homebrew or curl installs.

Setup also writes `"autoupdate": false` into `opencode.jsonc` in both modes' config sets, so opencode does not update itself past the tested version. Versions move only when a Hive release does: run `habithive update`. If the running opencode is not the tested version, the launcher and the in-app plugin each show a one-line warning and carry on.

Hive needs OpenCode 1. OpenCode 2 has a new plugin format and oh-my-openagent's agents do not run on it. **Do not run `opencode upgrade --major`** (opencode 1.19 suggests it). If OpenCode 2 is installed, the launcher, `habithive status` and `habithive setup` say so and show how to go back; setup never runs `opencode upgrade` against it. Use the command for how you installed OpenCode 2:

- npm: `npm rm -g @opencode/cli`, then `habithive setup`
- Homebrew: `brew uninstall opencode-v2`, then `habithive setup`
- curl installer: `curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash -s -- --version 1.19.4`

Sessions created under OpenCode 2 may not open in OpenCode 1. Per-version findings are in [docs/COMPATIBILITY.md](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md).

## Uninstall

Switch to the mode whose config you want to keep first: deleting `~/.habithive` also deletes the other mode's stored config set.

```sh
habithive complex      # switches back to complex mode; quit opencode when it opens
npm rm -g habithive-code
npm rm -g @fission-ai/openspec                         # optional
rm -rf ~/.local/share/openspec/schemas/intent-driven   # optional
rm -rf ~/.habithive
```

Then remove the Hive and oh-my-openagent entries from `~/.config/opencode/tui.json` and `opencode.jsonc`. Details: [Files and safety](docs/guide/08-files-and-safety.md#uninstall).

- Toolchain versions are pinned and move only with a Hive release: opencode 1.19.4, oh-my-openagent 4.19.1, OpenSpec 1.5.0. Setup moves your installs to these versions.
- opencode self-update is turned off (`autoupdate: false`). Use `habithive update`.
- OpenCode 2 is not supported. Do not run `opencode upgrade --major`; complex mode and the model tree do not work on OpenCode 2.
- Launching `habithive` no longer repairs or rewrites opencode config. Repair happens in `habithive setup` and `habithive update`.

### Added

- `habithive update`: installs the latest `habithive-code` from npm, then re-applies the release pins and config steps. Your mode, model overrides, baseline and other config are kept. For a source checkout it prints `git pull` instructions instead.
- Update notice: the TUI plugin checks npm at most once every 24 hours (cached, silent offline) and shows a toast when a newer version exists.
- `hive` as a second name for the `habithive` command. Setup warns if another `hive` program is on PATH.
- `habithive spec init`: sets up a project with OpenSpec and the `intent-driven` schema. See the spec workflow chapter in `docs/guide/`.
- The `intent-driven` schema ships with the package and is installed to OpenSpec's user-level data directory by setup and update.
- OmniRoute provider with 38 `auto/*` models, installed by setup and update. No API key is shipped; add yours with `/connect`. `habithive --gateway <ip>` sets the gateway address for a developer.
- "This screen (live)" in `/hive-models`, which opens opencode's native model picker with no relaunch.
- OpenCode 2 detection in the launcher, `habithive status` and setup, with recovery steps for npm, brew and curl installs. When setup moves opencode to the tested version, it tells you to ignore opencode's `opencode upgrade --major` suggestion.
- A warning when a chosen model will be rerouted by oh-my-openagent (Sisyphus with older GPT models, Hephaestus with non-GPT models).
- `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` (tested version set and findings), the user guide in `docs/guide/`, and this changelog.
- Tests for the config editor, versions, update, OmniRoute, OpenSpec, spec init and a package check that fails on any IPv4 address in published files.

### Changed

- Mode switching renames between two complete config file sets (`~/.habithive/modes/<mode>/`) instead of editing config. A launch in the active mode writes nothing. The mode is recorded in `~/.habithive/mode`.
- All setup and update writes go through a safe JSONC editor: comments and trailing commas are tolerated, strings are never altered, nothing is written if the file does not parse, a timestamped backup is made first, and unchanged files are not rewritten. A file Hive changes is saved as plain JSON: every setting is kept, comments and layout are not (the backup keeps them).
- Main-agent model changes are automatic: Hive writes config, relaunches into the same session, then moves the on-screen agent to the chosen model. If that cannot be confirmed, the native picker opens with the model at the top of Recent.
- Relaunch is safer: never while a permission or question prompt is open, works on older plugin APIs, does not quit an opencode that `habithive` did not start, and tells you when the quit did not happen.
- Menu labels show the configured model and mark changes that wait for a relaunch.
- "ALL" is now "Everything (agents + tiers)".
- Setup upgrades an existing graphify install; OpenSpec is held at the pin.
- OmniRoute entries are Hive-owned: name, adapter and the 38 models are reset on each setup or update. Models you added and any existing `apiKey` or base URL are kept.
- The published package contains no gateway address. OmniRoute is installed with the placeholder `http://localhost:20128/v1`.

### Fixed

- A trailing comma in `opencode.jsonc` no longer causes your config to be overwritten with a minimal file.
- Glob strings such as `"src/**/*.ts"` and URLs are no longer corrupted by comment stripping.
- Launching `habithive` and switching modes no longer rewrite your config, so they no longer remove your comments.
- Fresh install: with no `oh-my-openagent.json`, the baseline was empty and every model change was refused ("baseline not captured"). An empty baseline is now valid and is re-captured once the file gains content Hive did not write.
- "Main agent - this screen" never took effect, and "All main agents" skipped the agent on screen. Both are replaced by the automatic flow above.
- A misleading "run: habithive update" line on OpenCode 2, and `habithive setup` trying `opencode upgrade <pin>` against OpenCode 2.
- A user-edited copy of the `intent-driven` schema is backed up to `~/.habithive/schema-backups/`, not into OpenSpec's schemas folder, which lists every folder as a schema.

### Removed

- The "Quick" section of the model tree, including "Main agent - this screen".
- The `--minimal` install mode (see Breaking).
- The `/model` command registration (see Breaking).

### Upgrading from 0.2.x

`habithive update` does not exist in 0.2.4 or earlier. Upgrade once by hand, then use it from then on:

```bash
npm i -g habithive-code@latest && habithive setup
habithive update      # for every later release
```

Check that `node --version` is 20.19 or later first. If you were on a newer opencode than 1.19.4, setup moves it to the pin. If you ran `opencode upgrade --major`, follow the recovery steps that `habithive status` prints.

Setup leaves you in complex mode. If you used simple mode, run `habithive simple` once afterwards; your simple-mode settings are kept.

Setup saves the opencode config files it changes (usually `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`) as plain JSON. Every setting is kept, but comments and layout are removed. The original is saved next to the file as `opencode.jsonc.habithive-bak-<timestamp>`. Hive keeps only the newest 5 backups per file, so copy out any comments you want soon after upgrading.

| A | no `apiKey` | unset | `connect-key-123` | `Bearer connect-key-123` | The `/connect` key is used. |
| B | `apiKey: "{env:OMNIROUTE_API_KEY}"` | unset | `connect-key-123` | none (no header) | The empty `{env:}` result shadows the `/connect` key. |
| C | `apiKey: "{env:OMNIROUTE_API_KEY}"` | `env-key-456` | `connect-key-123` | `Bearer env-key-456` | The config `apiKey` wins over auth.json. |
| D | no `apiKey` | unset | none | none (no header) | The provider is still allowed (defined in config) and the request is sent unauthenticated. |

Conclusion: a provider block with no `apiKey` line plus a key saved through `/connect` is sufficient. A leftover `apiKey: "{env:OMNIROUTE_API_KEY}"` line breaks `/connect` unless that variable is exported.

Guidance: if your `opencode.jsonc` still has `"apiKey": "{env:OMNIROUTE_API_KEY}"` under `provider.omniroute.options`, delete that line (or export the variable) so the `/connect` key is sent.

## OpenCode 2

Date: 2026-10-23
Change: `hive-opencode-v2-guard` (ADR-0010; research: `review/opencode-2/SUMMARY.md`)

### Status

- OpenCode 2 is stable: 2.0.0 shipped 2026-09-11, current 2.1.3 (npm `@opencode/cli`, Homebrew `anomalyco/tap/opencode-v2`).
- OpenCode 1 is still patched (`opencode-ai` 1.19.4, 2026-10-22), no end-of-life date announced.
- `opencode upgrade --major` (from 1.19) moves an install to OpenCode 2: npm-family installs swap `opencode-ai` for `@opencode/cli`, brew swaps the formula, curl replaces the binary; data is migrated in place.

### What breaks

| Area | On OpenCode 2 |
|------|---------------|
| oh-my-openagent | 4.19.1 fails to load; 5.x loads only a stub that toasts a redirect to a separate product (OmO Native). Agents, tools and hooks do not run. **Complex mode and the model tree have no engine.** |
| Plugin module | The v1 `{ id, tui }` shape is gone (new `{ id, setup(context) }`); the Hive plugin does not load (non-fatal). TUI plugin wiring moves to `cli.json`; no `home_logo` slot. |
| CLI | `--version` prints `opencode v2.x`; `--model`, `--agent`, `--fork`, `--pure` are rejected; `opencode upgrade 1.19.0` fails (404), so Hive cannot downgrade through OpenCode 2. |
| Credentials, process model | `/connect` keys move to SQLite; the TUI is a client of a shared background service. |
| Unchanged | Config files and merge order, `autoupdate`, `provider` blocks, `model.json`. |

### Decision

ADR-0010: Hive stays on OpenCode 1 (pinned, ADR-0003). OpenCode 2 is unsupported until a complex-mode engine exists on it (OmO Native is evaluated separately).

Behaviour:

- The launcher replaces the "not the tested version" line with a notice (OpenCode 2 detected, Hive needs OpenCode 1, recovery steps for the detected install method) and still starts opencode.
- `habithive status` adds a line saying OpenCode 2 is not supported.
- `habithive setup` and `habithive reconcile` (so `habithive update`) never run `opencode upgrade` against OpenCode 2; they print the recovery steps and continue.
- Install method comes from the resolved path of `opencode` on PATH (npm, brew, curl, else unknown, which lists all three). Hive never uninstalls or reinstalls opencode for you.

- npm: `npm rm -g @opencode/cli`, then `habithive setup`
- Homebrew: `brew uninstall opencode-v2`, then `habithive setup`
- curl installer: `curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash -s -- --version 1.19.0`

Sessions created under OpenCode 2 may not open in OpenCode 1 (OpenCode 2 migrates data in place; the reverse is not verified).

## OpenSpec 1.5.0 pin

Hive pins `@fission-ai/openspec` at 1.5.0. OpenSpec 1.14.x rejects `generates` paths containing `..`, and the intent-driven schema's ADR step writes outside the change folder (`../../adr/`), so the schema fails validation there. 1.5.0 accepts it. `habithive setup` installs the pin and copies the bundled intent-driven schema to the user-level OpenSpec schemas folder; OpenSpec 1.5.0 needs Node 20.19 or newer. See ADR-0011.

# 1. Getting started

## What it is

Hive installs and wires opencode, oh-my-openagent, the Hive plugin, extra tools and skills with one command, then launches opencode in complex mode. This chapter takes you from nothing to a verified install. The command is `habithive`; `hive` is the same command.

## Prerequisites

| Need | Why |
|------|-----|
| Node.js 20.19 or newer | OpenSpec 1.5.0 requires it. Hive checks at start and exits with a message if Node is older. |
| Internet access | First setup fetches opencode, oh-my-openagent, OpenSpec and graphify. |
| `uv`, or Python 3.10+ with `pip` | Installs the graphify CLI. Without either (macOS's built-in Python is 3.9), setup installs `uv` with Homebrew if Homebrew is present; otherwise it skips graphify with a one-line note and continues. |

Upgrade Node with a version manager, for example:

```sh
nvm install 22
```

## Install

```sh
npm i -g habithive-code
```

If npm fails with `EACCES`, its global prefix is not writable. Do not use `sudo`. Use a user-owned prefix or a Node version manager:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.npm-global && npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"     # add to your shell profile
npm i -g habithive-code
```

On version 0.2.4 or earlier `habithive update` does not exist. Upgrade once with `npm i -g habithive-code@latest && habithive setup`. Setup leaves you in complex mode; if you used simple mode, run `habithive simple` once afterwards. Setup also removes comments from the config files it changes; the original is kept as a `.habithive-bak-<timestamp>` file next to each one (see [Files and safety](08-files-and-safety.md)).

## Run setup

```sh
habithive setup
```

Setup asks before installing opencode if it is missing (`--yes` or `-y` skips the question). It is always a full install; `--minimal` is ignored with a message. Steps, in order:

| Step | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| opencode | Installs `opencode-ai` at the pinned version. Another 1.x is moved to the pin: with `npm i -g opencode-ai@<pin>` when it was installed with npm, otherwise with `opencode upgrade <pin>`. OpenCode 2 is never touched; setup prints how to go back. |
| oh-my-openagent | Adds `oh-my-openagent@4.19.1` to the complex mode config. |
| Hive plugin | Adds the Hive plugin `file://` entry to `tui.json` in both modes. |
| autoupdate | Sets `"autoupdate": false` in `opencode.jsonc`. |
| OmniRoute | Adds or refreshes the OmniRoute provider (38 models) with a placeholder address. |
| Playwright MCP | Adds the `playwright` MCP server if absent. |
| OpenSpec | Installs `@fission-ai/openspec@1.5.0` if the installed version differs. |
| intent-driven schema | Copies the schema to `~/.local/share/openspec/schemas/intent-driven`. |
| graphify | Installs or upgrades `graphifyy` via `uv`, or `pip` on Python 3.10+. Installs `uv` with Homebrew when neither is available. |
| Skills | Copies bundled skills to `~/.config/opencode/skills/`. |

On the first setup Hive records complex mode in `~/.habithive/mode`. Running setup again is safe: it changes only what differs and writes nothing when everything is current. If a config file cannot be parsed, setup stops and prints `file:line:column`. If `hive` on your PATH is another program, setup warns; use `habithive`.

## First launch

```sh
habithive
```

This starts a new session in complex mode. Other forms:

```sh
habithive simple        # vanilla opencode
habithive -c            # continue the last session
habithive -s <id>       # continue a specific session
```

## Enable OmniRoute

Every install includes the OmniRoute provider pointing at `http://localhost:20128/v1`. If you are eligible, point it at your team's gateway, then add your key in opencode:

```sh
habithive --gateway <ip>
```

Pass the IP only; Hive adds `http://` and port 20128. Then run `/connect` in opencode, pick OmniRoute and paste your key. Hive never writes a key. See [OmniRoute](04-omniroute.md).

## Verify

```sh
habithive status        # prints "habithive: complex mode"
```

In opencode: `/habithive` opens the Hive menu and `/hive-models` opens the model tree. The home screen shows the HABITHIVE wordmark.

## Install from a source checkout

```sh
git clone https://repository.hclhealthcare.in/hive/habit-hive-code.git
cd habit-hive-code
npm test                        # every suite should report 0 failed
node bin/habithive.mjs status   # smoke test, nothing installed globally
npm i -g .
habithive setup
```

You need a GitLab account with access to the `hive` group. From a checkout, `habithive update` never reinstalls from npm; it prints `git -C <checkout> pull && habithive update`.

## Migrating from the previous package name

`habithive-code` replaces an earlier package with a different name and plugin entry. If the old one is still wired into any opencode config, both load and two wordmarks stack on the home screen. opencode reads plugins from the global config and from per-project configs (`opencode.json`, `opencode.jsonc`, `.opencode/opencode.json`), so clean both:

```sh
npm rm -g maliv-code
rm -rf ~/.maliv
find ~ -not -path "*/node_modules/*" -not -path "*/.git/*" -not -path "*/Library/*" \( -name "tui.json" -o -name "opencode.json" -o -name "opencode.jsonc" \) -print0 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -0 grep -l "maliv" 2>/dev/null \
  | while read -r f; do
      echo "cleaning: $f"
      node -e '
        const fs = require("fs");
        const p = process.argv[1];
        const raw = fs.readFileSync(p, "utf8");
        const c = JSON.parse(raw.replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, "").replace(/^\s*\/\/.*$/gm, ""));
        if (Array.isArray(c.plugin)) c.plugin = c.plugin.filter(e => !String(e).includes("maliv"));
        fs.writeFileSync(p, JSON.stringify(c, null, 2) + "\n");
      ' "$f"
    done
habithive setup
```

The script rewrites each file as plain JSON, so comments in those files are lost. If a cleaned file is tracked by git in a shared project, commit that fix, or teammates will bring the old entry back. Skip this section if you never had the old package.

# Modes: simple and complex

## What it is

Hive runs opencode in one of two modes. **Complex** mode loads oh-my-openagent (the multi-agent layer) plus Hive's plugin. **Simple** mode is vanilla opencode plus Hive's plugin, with oh-my-openagent off. You can start in either mode and switch at any time, from the shell or from inside opencode, without losing your session.

| | Simple | Complex |
|---|--------|---------|
| oh-my-openagent | off | on (pinned `oh-my-openagent@4.19.1`) |
| Hive plugin (`tui.json`) | on | on |
| Agents, categories, model tree | not used | available |
| Startup | fastest | loads the agent layer |

Complex is the default.

## Launching

`hive` is the same command as `habithive`.

| Command | Result |
|---------|--------|
| `habithive` | Complex mode, new session |
| `habithive simple` | Simple mode, new session |
| `habithive complex` | Complex mode, new session |
| `habithive -c` | Continue the last session (also `--continue`) |
| `habithive -s <id>` | Continue a specific session (also `--session <id>`) |
| `habithive new` | New session (the default; also `-n`, `--new`) |
| `habithive status` | Print the current mode and any queued switch |

Flags combine with a mode and any other arguments opencode accepts:

```bash
habithive simple -c
habithive complex -s <id>
habithive status
```

Output of `status` looks like `habithive: complex mode`, with ` · queued → simple` appended if an in-app switch is waiting.

On exit, Hive prints the resume commands (`habithive -c` and `habithive -s <id>`). Use those rather than opencode's own `opencode -s` hint so the right mode and plugin load.

## Switching inside opencode

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `/habithive-mode` | Opens the mode menu: switch to Simple or Complex |
| `/habithive` | Umbrella menu: model tree, switch mode, reset model overrides |

Choosing a mode queues the switch and quits opencode. The `habithive` launcher, which is still running, reopens opencode in the new mode and returns to **the same session** (`--session <id>`).

Details worth knowing:

- A brand-new session with no messages has no saved ID yet, so the relaunch opens a fresh session. Hive never uses `--continue` here, because that would reopen an older conversation.
- Switching only works when opencode was started by `habithive`. Otherwise Hive shows a toast with the command to run, for example `restart with habithive simple to switch mode`, and does not quit.
- If a permission or question prompt is open, Hive waits until you answer it before quitting.
- If opencode ignores the quit, a warning appears after 3 seconds: type `/exit` so Hive can reopen the session.

## How a switch works

Each mode owns **one complete set of config files**.

| Set | Location while active | Location while inactive |
|-----|-----------------------|-------------------------|
| Active mode | `~/.config/opencode/` (`opencode.jsonc`, `tui.json`) | n/a |
| Inactive mode | n/a | `~/.habithive/modes/<mode>/` |

Hive also manages `opencode.json` if it lists oh-my-openagent. The list of managed files is recorded in `~/.habithive/modes/files.json`.

- **A switch only renames files.** The active set moves to the store and the other set moves into `~/.config/opencode/`. File contents are not edited.
- **The first switch creates the other set, once,** by copying your active files and adding or removing the oh-my-openagent plugin entry. If either file cannot be parsed, the switch stops and names the file and line. Nothing is changed.
- **A normal launch writes no config.** Launching in the mode you are already in touches nothing.
- **Hive's record of the active mode** is `~/.habithive/mode`.

### Additions stay in one mode

Because the sets are independent, a change you make in one mode is not in the other. Add an MCP server, plugin or provider while in complex mode and it is absent in simple mode. Hive prints this reminder after each switch.

To carry a change across, copy it by hand into the other set's file. While in complex mode, the simple set sits in `~/.habithive/modes/simple/`:

```bash
# edit the stored file directly (this is the inactive mode's copy)
$EDITOR ~/.habithive/modes/simple/opencode.jsonc
```

Edit stored files only for the inactive mode. Do not edit them while that mode is active, because the active copy lives in `~/.config/opencode/`. Keep the oh-my-openagent entry out of the simple set.

`habithive setup` and `habithive update` apply Hive's own entries (plugin, pins, OmniRoute block) to both sets, so those stay aligned without manual work. See [07-updates-and-versions.md](07-updates-and-versions.md).

## Recovering from an interrupted switch

A switch writes a journal (`~/.habithive/switch.journal`) before renaming anything. If Hive is killed mid-switch, the next `habithive` launch finishes the switch, or rolls it back if it cannot, and prints one of:

- `completed interrupted switch to <mode> mode`
- `rolled back interrupted switch to <mode> mode (...); still <mode> mode`
- `could not recover interrupted switch (...); see ~/.habithive/switch.journal`

In the last case, compare `~/.habithive/modes/` with `~/.config/opencode/`, restore the files by hand, then delete the journal. An unreadable journal produces a similar message. See [09-troubleshooting.md](09-troubleshooting.md).

# Model tree

## What it is

The model tree is a menu inside opencode for choosing which model each oh-my-openagent agent and task tier uses. Open it with `/hive-models` (alias `/hivemodels`) or from the `/habithive` umbrella menu. It is meant for complex mode, where oh-my-openagent is loaded. The on-screen model is changed live through opencode's own picker; everything else is saved to a config file and takes effect after a relaunch, which Hive performs for you.

## The rows

Rows appear in this order. Each row shows the configured model, such as `→ provider/model`, or `→ (default)` when nothing is set.

| Group | Row | Sets |
|-------|-----|------|
| Live | **This screen (live)** | Opens opencode's own model picker. Instant, no relaunch. |
| Everything | **★ Everything (agents + tiers)** | One model for every agent and every tier |
| Main agents (primary) | **★ All main agents** | The four main agents below |
| | Sisyphus — ultraworker | `sisyphus` |
| | Prometheus — plan builder | `prometheus` |
| | Atlas — plan executor | `atlas` |
| | Hephaestus — deep (GPT-only) | `hephaestus` |
| Subagents | **★ All sub agents** | The seven subagents below |
| | Oracle — deep reasoning / debugging | `oracle` |
| | Explore — codebase search | `explore` |
| | Librarian — external docs | `librarian` |
| | Multimodal-looker — images / visual | `multimodal-looker` |
| | Metis — plan consultant | `metis` |
| | Momus — plan critic | `momus` |
| | Sisyphus-Junior — worker | `sisyphus-junior` |
| Categories (tiers) | `ultrabrain`, `deep`, `quick`, `visual-engineering`, `artistry`, `writing`, `unspecified-low`, `unspecified-high` | One tier each |

Picking a row opens a filterable list of every model from your connected providers. Choose one, or choose **Clear override (use default)** to remove the override for that row. Group rows show `→ all: <model>` when every member agrees and `→ (mixed)` when they differ.

## Precedence

The most specific setting wins:

```
agent  >  category  >  all  >  default
```

- **agent**: an override on one agent.
- **category**: an override on a tier.
- **all**: the "Everything" row.
- **default**: your original `oh-my-openagent.json`, saved as the baseline (see below).

Two behaviors follow from how Hive compiles the settings:

- Choosing a model on **Everything** replaces any agent and category overrides, so one model really applies everywhere.
- If any category override exists, agents without their own override drop their model and inherit from their category, which is how oh-my-openagent cascades.

## What is live and what needs a relaunch

| Change | Applies |
|--------|---------|
| This screen (live) | Immediately. It is opencode's own picker. |
| Any other row | After a relaunch, which Hive performs (same session) |

oh-my-openagent reads its config once at startup. Writing the file does not change a running process, so Hive saves your choice, quits opencode, and the `habithive` launcher reopens the same session. A row saved but not yet in effect shows ` · pending relaunch` after its model.

### Main agent models after relaunch

opencode restores a session's last-used model when you reopen it, overriding config. To make a main-agent change (Sisyphus, Prometheus, Atlas, Hephaestus, the main group, or Everything) show up on screen, Hive:

1. Reorders opencode's recent-models list so the old model and the new one are adjacent.
2. Leaves a short-lived marker (valid 10 minutes).
3. After the relaunch, triggers opencode's recent-model cycle exactly once to move the active agent to the new model, and shows a toast such as `sisyphus → provider/model`.

If the cycle cannot run, Hive opens the native model picker and shows `select <model> to apply it to <agent>`. Pick the model there.

Subagents and tiers never change the on-screen model, so they skip this step.

## Safety

- **Not started by `habithive`:** Hive does not quit. It saves the change and shows `saved — restart with habithive -c to apply`.
- **Prompt open:** if a permission or question prompt is open, Hive waits until it is answered, then quits.
- **Quit ignored:** after 3 seconds a warning asks you to type `/exit` so the session can reopen.
- **Model rules:** oh-my-openagent enforces them, not Hive. Sisyphus does not accept most GPT models: among GPT models only `gpt-5.4` and newer, `gpt-5-codex` and `gpt-5.3-codex` are accepted (non-GPT models are fine). Hephaestus is GPT-only unless your config sets `allow_non_gpt_model`. If you pick a model that breaks a rule, Hive warns beforehand: oh-my-openagent will reroute and the agent keeps its previous model.

## Reset

`/habithive` then **Reset all model overrides** clears every override and rewrites `oh-my-openagent.json` from the baseline. Relaunch to apply. It does not quit for you.

## Where settings live

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `~/.habithive/overrides.json` | Your overrides: `all`, `categories`, `agents` |
| `~/.habithive/baseline.json` | Snapshot of your original `oh-my-openagent.json`, the "default" and the Reset target |
| `~/.config/opencode/oh-my-openagent.json` | What oh-my-openagent reads. Hive compiles it from overrides plus baseline. |
| `~/.habithive/oh-my-openagent.first-backup.json` | Copy of the file as found when the baseline was first captured |
| `~/.local/state/opencode/model.json` | opencode's own picker state; Hive only reorders its `recent` list |

On a fresh install, where `oh-my-openagent.json` does not exist yet, the baseline is empty and Hive writes only your overrides. If you later edit the file yourself, Hive recaptures the baseline once rather than overwriting your changes. Edit overrides through the menu, not by hand in `oh-my-openagent.json`, because Hive rewrites that file when you apply a change.

# OmniRoute gateway

## What it is

OmniRoute is your team's model gateway. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so opencode talks to it through the `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` adapter. Hive ships an `omniroute` provider with a fixed set of 38 models, installed for everyone with a placeholder address (`http://localhost:20128/v1`). The package contains no real gateway address. A developer becomes eligible by pointing Hive at the gateway and adding a key.

## Enable OmniRoute on your machine

Get the gateway IP from your team, then run:

```bash
habithive --gateway <ip>
```

Behavior:

- Takes the IP only. Hive builds `http://<ip>:20128/v1` itself.
- Writes the address into the OmniRoute block of **both** mode sets (see [02-modes.md](02-modes.md)), adding the block if it is missing.
- Prints `OmniRoute enabled (...)` and the files updated, or `already set`.
- **Exits without launching opencode.**
- Rejects input that is not a bare dotted IPv4 address: a scheme or port (`pass only the IP address: habithive --gateway <ip>`), out-of-range or malformed numbers (`not a valid IPv4 address: ...`), or no value (`usage: habithive --gateway <ip>`).
- Stops and names the file, line and column if a config file cannot be parsed.

## Add your key

Start opencode and run `/connect`, choose OmniRoute, and enter your API key. opencode stores it; Hive never writes or reads secrets. No model is made a default: choose OmniRoute models in the model picker or the [model tree](03-model-tree.md).

Who may use the gateway is controlled in the OmniRoute dashboard. Hive has no command to disable access; to remove a developer, change their eligibility there.

## What updates do and do not touch

`habithive update`, `habithive reconcile` and `habithive setup` keep the block current.

| Hive keeps aligned | Hive never touches |
|--------------------|--------------------|
| Provider `name` (`OmniRoute`) | The address (`options.baseURL`) once set |
| Adapter (`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`) | Any `apiKey` in the block |
| The 38 shipped model entries (names and limits) | Models you added yourself |
| | Everything outside `provider.omniroute` |

An update never changes the address. If the address is empty or missing, it is reset to the placeholder.

### Old `apiKey` line

If your block has `"apiKey": "{env:OMNIROUTE_API_KEY}"` from an older hand-copied config, either export `OMNIROUTE_API_KEY` or delete that line. With the variable unset, opencode sends no key and ignores the one saved by `/connect`. Hive does not add or remove that line. Evidence is in [../COMPATIBILITY.md](../COMPATIBILITY.md).

# 05. Spec workflow

## What it is

Hive ships a spec workflow built on OpenSpec and a custom schema called `intent-driven`. A change moves through a fixed chain of written artifacts (proposal, specs, design, ADR, tasks) before any code is written, and the agent then implements the task list. `habithive setup` installs everything you need. `habithive spec init` prepares a project to use it.

## Why a spec workflow

- The intent (why) is written down before the implementation (how).
- Behaviour is described as testable GIVEN/WHEN/THEN scenarios, not prose.
- Long-lived architectural decisions are kept in the repo as ADRs, so the next change can read them.
- The agent works from a checklist and marks progress, so a session can be resumed.

## OpenSpec is pinned at 1.5.0

Setup and update install exactly `@fission-ai/openspec@1.5.0`. A newer install is moved down to it. Newer releases (1.14.x was tested) reject the `intent-driven` schema, because its ADR step writes outside the change folder, and silently fall back to the default `spec-driven` schema. OpenSpec 1.5.0 needs Node.js 20.19 or later, which is why Hive requires it too.

The pin moves only with a Hive release. See [../COMPATIBILITY.md](../COMPATIBILITY.md).

## The intent-driven chain

```
proposal -> specs -> design -> adr -> tasks -> apply
```

| Step | Produces | Requires | Contents |
|------|----------|----------|----------|
| proposal | `proposal.md` | nothing | Why (1-2 sentences), What Changes (mark breaking items **BREAKING**), Capabilities (new and modified, kebab-case names), Impact |
| specs | `specs/<capability>/spec.md` | proposal | One delta spec per capability. Requirements and scenarios in Gherkin style |
| design | `design.md` | proposal | Context, Goals / Non-Goals, Decisions (with alternatives), Risks / Trade-offs, Migration Plan, Open Questions |
| adr | `<repo>/adr/NNNN-title.md` | design | New Architecture Decision Records for long-term decisions |
| tasks | `tasks.md` | specs, adr | Numbered groups of `- [ ] X.Y` checkbox tasks |
| apply | code | tasks | Work through pending tasks and tick them off |

### Specs

Each spec file is an OpenSpec delta. Use these headings exactly so archive can merge them:

- `## ADDED Requirements`, `## MODIFIED Requirements` (paste the full updated requirement, not a partial diff), `## REMOVED Requirements` (needs **Reason** and **Migration**), `## RENAMED Requirements` (`FROM:` / `TO:`).
- Each requirement is `### Requirement: <name>` and needs at least one scenario.
- Each scenario is `#### Scenario: <name>` (four hashes) with GIVEN, WHEN and THEN steps, plus AND or BUT for follow-ons.

```markdown
## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Export as CSV
Users can export the report table.

#### Scenario: Export with rows
- **GIVEN** a report with three rows
- **WHEN** the user chooses Export
- **THEN** a CSV file with a header and three rows is downloaded
```

Write observable outcomes in THEN steps. Do not create `.feature` files.

### Design

Include `design.md` only when it helps: cross-cutting changes, new dependencies or data models, security, performance or migration concerns, or real ambiguity. Before writing, the agent reads the existing ADRs and keeps the design consistent with those in force. If a design needs to revisit an ADR, it lists that under Open Questions rather than editing the ADR.

## ADR rules

- ADRs live in the repository's top-level `adr/` folder, beside `openspec/`. Never under `openspec/` and never inside a change folder.
- File name: `NNNN-kebab-title.md`, a four-digit sequence one higher than the highest in use. Numbers are never reused.
- ADRs are immutable once accepted. Do not edit a prior ADR: not its status, body or date.
- To change a decision, write a new ADR with status `accepted, supersedes ADR-NNNN` and a `Supersedes:` field naming the old one. The old ADR stays as history.
- An ADR is in force unless a later ADR supersedes it. The agent walks the `Supersedes:` links to find the set in force.
- Only record decisions that are long-term, affect future changes, and are not already covered. If nothing qualifies, no ADR is created.

An ADR has: Status, Date, Supersedes, Context and Problem Statement, Considered Options, Decision Outcome, Consequences.

## Set up a project: `habithive spec init`

Run it from the project root (or pass a folder):

```bash
cd my-project
habithive spec init
```

It requires the `openspec` command on PATH (`habithive setup` installs it). It then:

1. Runs `openspec init --tools opencode`, creating `openspec/`, the opencode slash commands and skills.
2. Copies the `intent-driven` schema into `openspec/schemas/intent-driven/` so it is committed with your code.
3. Sets `schema: intent-driven` in `openspec/config.yaml`.
4. Runs `openspec schema validate intent-driven` and prints `ok` or `failed`.

Then commit `openspec/` and `.opencode/`.

If `openspec/config.yaml` already exists, Hive changes nothing. It prints the current schema, and if that is not `intent-driven` it prints how to switch:

```bash
openspec schema fork intent-driven intent-driven
# then set `schema: intent-driven` in openspec/config.yaml
```

## Slash commands

`openspec init --tools opencode` creates these commands in the project's `.opencode/commands/`, in both modes:

| Command | Does |
|---------|------|
| `/opsx-propose` | Creates a change and generates the artifacts in one step |
| `/opsx-explore` | Think through an idea or problem before or during a change |
| `/opsx-apply` | Implements `tasks.md`, ticking checkboxes |
| `/opsx-sync` | Syncs delta specs into `openspec/specs/` without archiving |
| `/opsx-archive` | Archives a finished change |

There are no global `/opsx` commands. They exist only in projects that have been initialised. Matching skills are created under `.opencode/skills/`.

## Worked example

```text
/opsx-propose export-report-csv     # change folder + proposal, specs, design, tasks
```

1. Review `openspec/changes/export-report-csv/proposal.md` and the spec scenarios. Edit them until they say what you want.
2. Check `design.md`, and the new file in `adr/` if a long-term decision was made.
3. Run `/opsx-apply`. The agent implements tasks and marks `- [ ]` as `- [x]`.
4. Validate, then archive:

```bash
openspec validate export-report-csv --type change --strict
```

```text
/opsx-sync       # optional: merge specs now
/opsx-archive    # finish and archive the change
```

If a change name is ambiguous, `openspec list --json` lists the changes.

## Refresh a project's schema copy

Setup and update refresh the user-level schema only. A project keeps its own copy in `openspec/schemas/intent-driven/` and `habithive spec init` will not overwrite it. To take a newer shipped version, replace the project copy with the user-level one and review the diff before committing:

```bash
cp -R ~/.local/share/openspec/schemas/intent-driven/. openspec/schemas/intent-driven/
```

## Where the user-level schema lives

Setup and update install the schema to OpenSpec's data directory so every project can resolve it:

| Platform | Path |
|----------|------|
| macOS, Linux | `~/.local/share/openspec/schemas/intent-driven/` |
| With `XDG_DATA_HOME` set | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/openspec/schemas/intent-driven/` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\openspec\schemas\intent-driven\` |

Hive owns this folder. If you edited it, setup moves your copy to `~/.habithive/schema-backups/intent-driven-<timestamp>` before installing the shipped one. Make lasting changes in a project copy instead.
